```{=html}
<p class="lx-eyebrow">SPP hourly demand, 2025: baselines, a learned model and a band, scored by time</p>
<ol>
<li>Split by time: train on 6,383 hours (8 January to 30 September 2025), choose on October (744 hours), test once on November (721).</li>
<li>On October, same hour yesterday misses by 1,126 MW on average (MAPE 3.6%); same hour last week by 2,232 MW; the latest hour held flat by 3,186 MW.</li>
<li>Persistence (the reading h hours earlier, issued every hour), October error in % of each series' 2025 maximum, 1 and 12 hours ahead: demand 1.4 and 10.0; wind 2.8 and 17.5; solar 6.3 and 48.7.</li>
<li>Solar is zero in 377 of 744 October hours of the cleaned series, which sets night hours to zero.</li>
<li>The best of 16 feature mixes on October: same hour yesterday + same hour last week + the latest actual + Saturday and Sunday, 1,083 MW, 3.8% better than same hour yesterday.</li>
<li>Leaks: adding the hour before scores 670 MW on October, adding the day's actual average 822 MW; at 00:00 neither is known for every hour of the day.</li>
<li>November, opened once: 981 MW against 1,070 MW for same hour yesterday (8.3% better).</li>
<li>An 80% band from October's misses, pooled over all hours (−1,801 MW to +1,861 MW), holds 83.1% of November's hours; its pinball loss is 398.1 MW.</li>
<li>The three worst November days (Sunday 30 November, Monday 10 November, Thursday 27 November) hold 25% of the month's absolute error.</li>
</ol>

<div class="lx-datanote"><svg class="lx-ic" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" aria-hidden="true"><circle cx="12" cy="12" r="8.5"/><path d="M12 11v5M12 8v.2"/></svg><ul>
<li><b>Data:</b> real hourly demand, wind and solar of the Southwest Power Pool (SPP) in 2025, as reported to <a href="https://www.eia.gov/electricity/gridmonitor/">EIA-930</a> (accessed 2 Nov 2026).</li>
<li><b>Cleaning:</b> done afterwards, with the whole year in hand: 699 of 2025's 8,760 demand hours were repaired from the day-ahead forecast scaled to actuals on both sides, and frozen wind and solar readings filled.</li>
<li><b>Solar at night:</b> the cleaned series sets it to zero for hours ending 23 to 5, hours whose monthly median is zero, and hours with the sun below the horizon at SPP's approximate center.</li>
<li><b>So:</b> a demonstration on cleaned data, not an operational backtest. Inputs are not exactly what was known at 00:00, and repaired hours are scored with the rest; the data do not mark them.</li>
<li><b>Scale:</b> each series is stored in thousandths of its 2025 maximum; wind and solar stay so. Demand is that share of SPP's 2025 peak hour, 54,411 MW, so values are rounded to about 54 MW.</li>
<li><b>Clock:</b> Central time with daylight saving: 9 March has 23 hours and 2 November 25. A forecast is issued at 00:00 for every hour of that day.</li>
<li><b>Same hour:</b> the same clock hour on the day (or week) before. A clock hour that occurs twice (2 November) is read as the later one; a missing one (9 March), as the hour before it.</li>
</ul></div>
<p class="lx-hint" style="margin-top:.6rem">About 40 guided minutes in nine steps. Every forecast is fitted in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere. Need a refresher on MAE and bands? <a href="04-forecasts.html">Lesson 4</a>.</p>
```

## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="m10-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Baseline first</dt><dd>A simple rule, such as same hour yesterday, that a model must beat on the same hours.</dd>
<dt>Split by time</dt><dd>Train on the past, choose on the next month, test once on the month after; never shuffle hours.</dd>
<dt>Known at 00:00</dt><dd>Every input must exist when the forecast is issued; a later actual is a leak.</dd>
<dt>Skill</dt><dd>One minus the model's MAE over the baseline's, on the same hours.</dd>
<dt>Band and pinball loss</dt><dd>Coverage says how often reality lands inside; pinball loss also charges for width.</dd>
<dt>Bad days</dt><dd>A month's average hides the few days that hold much of the error.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>The formulas: rules, the regression, skill and pinball loss</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **Symbols.** $t$ an hour; $y_t$ its actual demand and $\hat y_t$ a forecast of it; $x_t$ the list of inputs for hour $t$, starting with a 1 for the intercept; $w$ one weight per input; $X$ every training hour's $x_t$, one row each; $^\top$ the transpose ([K6](k06-vectors-matrices.html)); $\tau$ a quantile level and $\hat q$ the forecast's quantile at that level.
- **Horizon.** A forecast issued at 00:00, the end of the day before's last hour $t_0$, for hour $t$ has horizon $h = t - t_0$, 1 to 24 (25 on 2 November). An input is allowed only if it is known at $t_0$.
- **Baselines.** Persistence $\hat y_t = y_{t_0}$; same hour yesterday: $y$ at the same clock hour the day before (24 hours earlier on most days, 23 or 25 next to a clock change); same hour last week: the same clock hour seven days before (the seasonal naive rule).
- **A weighted sum.** With $w = (2,\ 0.6,\ 0.3)$ and $x_t = (1,\ 40,\ 38)$, the intercept's 1 and then same hour yesterday and last week in GW, $\hat y_t = 2 + 0.6 \times 40 + 0.3 \times 38 = 37.4$ GW (illustrative numbers).
- **Regression.** $\hat y_t = w^\top x_t$, with $w$ minimizing $\sum_t (y_t - w^\top x_t)^2$ over the training hours: the normal equations $X^\top X\, w = X^\top y$, solved by Cholesky as in [M9](m09-surrogates-uq.html).
- **Skill.** $1 - \text{MAE}_\text{model} / \text{MAE}_\text{baseline}$ on the same hours; 0 is no better than the baseline.
- **Band.** Quantiles $q_\tau$ of October's misses $y_t - \hat y_t$, pooled over all hours, give the band $\hat y_t + q_\tau$; the 80% band runs from $q_{0.1}$ to $q_{0.9}$.
- **Pinball loss** at level $\tau$: $\tau (y - \hat q)$ if $y \ge \hat q$, else $(1 - \tau)(\hat q - y)$. At the 90th percentile, a 100 MW miss above the forecast quantile costs 90 MW; the same miss below it costs 10 MW. The page averages it over the 19 levels 5% to 95%. It is a proper score: in expectation, no band beats the true quantiles.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>What the lab adds, and what real forecasters use</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **Model ladder.** Baseline, then linear regression, then gradient-boosted trees, then neural networks; each must still beat the baseline on held-out hours.
- **Gradient-boosted trees.** Many small if-then trees, each fitted to the misses of those before it, then added up.
- **A neural network.** Weighted sums of the inputs, each passed through a simple bend, then summed again; it can learn curved links a weighted sum cannot.
- **In the lab.** Gradient boosting and a small neural network on this page's features and split.
- **Weather.** Real day-ahead load forecasts use temperature forecasts; actual temperatures as inputs would be a leak, an oracle bound at best.
- **Rolling origin.** One test month is a small sample: refit and test month after month, and report the spread.
- **Further reading.** Hyndman and Athanasopoulos's free textbook covers baselines, accuracy and intervals in depth.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
</div>
```

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="m10-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="fancy" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A learned model easily beats a simple rule.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. The best of 16 linear mixes beat same hour yesterday by 3.8% on October and 8.3% on November. Report skill against the baseline, not the model alone.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="toogood" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A model that scores 670 MW where the best fair one scores 1,083 MW is simply better.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. It used the hour before each forecast hour: known at 00:00 for the day's first hour, unavailable for every later one. An unexpectedly good score is a reason to check for leakage.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="wide" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “The band that holds the most hours is the best band.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. At twice October's width the 80% band held 98.6% of November's hours, but its pinball loss was the worst of the widths tried. Check coverage and quantile scores together; choose a band on validation data, then report the test.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="m10">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="skill" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">A model's MAE is 950 MW; same hour yesterday's is 1,000 MW on the same hours. Its skill score?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">95%</li><li data-value="b">5%</li><li data-value="c">50 MW</li><li data-value="d">−5%</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>5%: 1 − 950 ÷ 1,000 = 0.05.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="lag" data-answer="c">
<p class="lx-qtext">A forecast issued at 00:00 on 14 October for the hour ending 18:00 on 14 October. Which input is allowed?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">Demand at 17:00 on 14 October</li><li data-value="b">The actual temperature on 14 October</li><li data-value="c">Demand at 18:00 on 13 October</li><li data-value="d">The average demand of 14 October</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Demand at 18:00 on 13 October: 24 hours before the target, and already known at 00:00 on 14 October. The others lie after the forecast is issued.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
```
